lines.text: Between two rivers, people built the first cities, wrote the first words and raised the first empires. This is Iraq, the land of Mesopotamia.
It begins with water. The Euphrates, the longest river of western Asia, flows down from Turkey through Syria and Iraq.
Beside it runs the Tigris. Between the two lay Mesopotamia, the land between the rivers, where farming could feed great cities.
On the banks of the Tigris, a settlement grew that would one day be Nineveh, capital of the Assyrians.
In the south, the Sumerians built rival city-states, dug canals, raised temple towers and invented writing on clay.
Uruk was one of the first large cities in the world, where cuneiform writing is thought to have begun.
At Ur, a great ziggurat rose over the city, and royal tombs full of treasure lay waiting to be found in the 1920s.
Then Sargon of Akkad joined the Sumerian cities with lands to the north and west, forging the first empire of Mesopotamia.
On clay tablets, scribes wrote the Epic of Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk who seeks to live forever after his friend dies. It is among the oldest stories we have.
The city of Babylon rose to lead a new kingdom, famed for its laws and its astronomers, who watched the sky for centuries.
Its greatest early king was Hammurabi, who made Babylon the leading power of Mesopotamia.
He had his laws carved on a stone pillar for all to see, setting out rules for trade, family, wages and punishment.
Later, from Nineveh, the Assyrian kings built an empire that conquered much of the Near East.
King Ashurbanipal gathered a library of clay tablets. When Nineveh burned, the fire baked them hard, and Gilgamesh survived.
Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar the Second, who captured Jerusalem and rebuilt his city in splendour, with the Ishtar Gate.
Greek writers told of terraced Hanging Gardens built for a king's wife. No Babylonian text mentions them, and the mystery remains.
In 331 BCE, on a plain in northern Iraq, Alexander the Great defeated the Persian king Darius, and the Persian Empire fell.
A thousand years later, a new Islamic dynasty, the Abbasids, moved the centre of their empire to Iraq.
On the Tigris they founded Baghdad in 762, soon one of the largest cities on Earth.
In its House of Wisdom, scholars put Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic, and pushed forward mathematics, astronomy and medicine.
In 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu Khan took Baghdad. The caliph was killed, and the city lost its libraries and much of its people.
Centuries later, after the First World War, Britain set up a Kingdom of Iraq under its mandate.
In 1932 Iraq became independent, a new country in the old land between the rivers.
In 1937 Saddam Hussein was born. He would rule Iraq for almost a quarter of a century.
In the summer of 1958, army officers overthrew the monarchy, and Iraq became a republic.
Ten years later the Baath party seized power, with Saddam Hussein rising inside it.
In 1980, now president, Saddam invaded Iran. Eight years of trench warfare and chemical weapons followed, with huge losses and borders barely changed.
Meanwhile his regime turned on Iraq's own Kurds in the Anfal campaign, a genocide.
In 1988, poison gas fell on the Kurdish town of Halabja, killing thousands.
In 1990 Iraq invaded Kuwait. A coalition led by the United States drove its forces out, the ground war lasting only days.
By the end of the century, a small jihadist group had formed that would later call itself the Islamic State.
In 2003 a US-led invasion removed Saddam Hussein. Years of insurgency and sectarian violence followed, and US forces left in 2011.
In 2014 the Islamic State seized much of Iraq, and the country fought for three years to take its cities back.
The hardest battle was for Mosul, retaken from the Islamic State in 2017.
Where writing and cities began, Iraq's long story is still being written.
